content: The SAPS Explosives Control Division acts as the second key regulator, focused on the security and licensing aspects of explosives. Their role is to prevent the diversion of explosives into illicit channels and to ensure that all entities handling these materials are properly authorized and compliant. Their enforcement powers include the ability to revoke licenses, seize materials, and initiate criminal proceedings for violations of the Explosives Act. Within this stringent regulatory context, specific safety challenges and trends in drilling and blasting demand constant attention. Historically, the most severe accidents have involved fly-rock (uncontrolled projectiles from a blast), misfires (where part of a charge fails to detonate), and exposure to toxic post-blast fumes like nitrogen oxides (NOx). The industry and its regulators have focused intensely on mitigating these risks. A significant critical debate within the safety profession revolves around the distinction between a "compliance culture" and a true "safety culture." A counterargument to the efficacy of the extensive regulatory framework is that it can inadvertently foster a "compliance culture," where a company's primary goal becomes "ticking the boxes" to pass audits and avoid regulatory sanctions. In such a culture, safety is seen as a bureaucratic exercise in paperwork and procedure, rather than a deeply held value that informs every decision and action. The argument is that over-regulation can stifle innovation and critical thinking, leading employees to simply "follow the book" rather than actively thinking about how to make their work safer. This creates a brittle safety system that can shatter in the face of an unexpected event. However, the modern approach to safety management provides a strong rebuttal to this concern. The evolution from simple rule-based systems to integrated safety management systems (ISMS), particularly those aligned with international standards like ISO 45001 (Occupational Health and Safety) , directly addresses this issue. These frameworks do not just mandate procedures; they require a holistic approach that embeds safety into the fabric of the organization. When properly implemented, such a system transforms compliance from a reactive, "tick-box" activity into a proactive, dynamic process of continuous learning and improvement.
